passage: Omkar, you asked why I keep a spare towel by my bed. Let me tell you. When I went to the hostel at fifteen, I cried quietly under my blanket at night so that the other boys wouldn't hear. I'm Hemant. I missed my mother, and the room smelled strange. No one knew. After two weeks, the warden's wife noticed my red eyes and sat with me one morning, and asked if I'd like to talk to the counsellor. I said yes. Crying alone isn't wrong. But if it goes on and you feel hopeless or you stop talking, tell someone you trust.

qa.q: What did Hemant keep by Hemant's bed?
qa.a: Hemant kept a spare towel by Hemant's bed.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when Hemant cried under Hemant's blanket?
qa.a: Hemant was lonely and missed Hemant's mother, and wanted to hide it. The strange smell of the room added to it.

qa.q: What advice would Hemant give Omkar about hidden crying?
qa.a: Crying alone is not wrong, but if it continues with hopelessness or silence, tell a trusted person. Hemant did and it helped.

qa.q: How did the warden's wife notice, and what did she do?
qa.a: She noticed Hemant's red eyes and sat with Hemant, offering the counsellor. She gave Hemant a choice.

grounding: A teenager cries quietly under a blanket to avoid being seen, and a trusted adult and counsellor help.

passage: The power cut had come with the storm, and the house was dark. Kishore lay under his blanket with his face in the pillow. He hadn't told anyone that he'd failed his trials. His shoulders shook silently. Gurleen, passing his door with a torch, heard a muffled sniff. She stopped, then knocked lightly. "Kishore? I'm not coming in unless you want." Nothing for a moment. Then, "You can come in." She sat on the floor by the bed, not saying anything. After a while he said, "I failed the trials." "I'm sorry. I'm here." She added that she could sit with him and, if it kept going, they could talk to Amma.

qa.q: What had come with the storm?
qa.a: The power cut had come with the storm.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling as he lay under the blanket?
qa.a: He was sad and disappointed about failing the trials, and hid it. His silent shaking shows he didn't want to be seen.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that helped?
qa.a: She knocked and asked permission before coming in, then sat quietly. She offered to talk to Amma if it kept going.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt hearing the sniff?
qa.a: She was probably worried, and careful not to intrude. She waited for his invitation.

grounding: A teenager cries silently under a blanket to avoid being seen, and a sibling offers company and a trusted adult.

passage:
For three weeks after moving to a new school in Chennai, Jatin had been quiet at dinner and went to his room straight after. He'd stopped playing cricket downstairs.
One night, his older sister Reena heard a small sound through the wall. She knocked softly and went in. Jatin was under his blanket, crying without making a sound.
"Jatin?"
He pulled the blanket tighter. "Go away."
Reena sat on the edge of the bed. "I won't tell you to stop. Is it the new school?"
After a long silence, he nodded. "I don't have anyone. Every day is the same."
Reena stayed with him. Then she said gently, "Can I tell Amma tonight? I think she'd want to help."
He nodded. Amma came in, sat with him till he slept, and the next morning called the school counsellor.

qa.q: How many weeks had Jatin been quiet at dinner?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling while crying under the blanket?
qa.a: Jatin felt lonely and sad after the move, with no friends at the new school.

qa.q: What did Reena do that was right?
qa.a: She stayed with him, didn't tell him to stop, and gently brought in Amma that same night.

qa.q: How did Amma respond when Reena told her?
qa.a: Amma sat with Jatin until he slept and called the school counsellor the next morning.

grounding: A teenager cries silently and withdraws for weeks, and a sibling brings in a trusted adult the same night.

passage:
"Sarita? Are you in there?"
"Go away, Arohi Didi."
"You've been in the bathroom for twenty minutes. I can hear you."
"I'm fine."
"You don't sound fine."
The door opened. Sarita's eyes were red. "It's the boards. I can't do it. Every night I cry and nobody knows."
"Every night?"
"For two weeks."
Arohi pulled her into a hug. "You don't have to hide it. That's too long to carry alone."
"Don't tell Mummy. She'll be upset."
"She'd be more upset if she didn't know. Let's tell her together. Right now, before dinner."
Sarita hesitated, then nodded.
They went to the kitchen together. Mummy put down the ladle, listened to everything, and hugged them both. "We'll talk to your class teacher and the counsellor tomorrow."

qa.q: How long had Sarita been crying every night?
qa.a: For two weeks.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling while crying in the bathroom?
qa.a: Sarita felt stressed and overwhelmed about the board exams, hiding the sadness from everyone.

qa.q: What did Arohi do that helped?
qa.a: She listened, hugged Sarita, and gently insisted on telling Mummy together that same evening.

qa.q: How did Mummy respond?
qa.a: Mummy listened, hugged them both, and planned to talk to the class teacher and counsellor the next day.

grounding: A teenager cries silently for weeks over exam stress, and an older sister helps her tell a trusted adult the same evening.

passage:
After Dadaji died when I was in Class 9, I didn't cry at the funeral. But every night, under my blanket, I cried silently so nobody would hear.
I stopped going to cricket. I stopped answering my friends' texts. I didn't want anyone to see how sad I was.
My cousin Parul noticed. She saw my puffy eyes one morning and didn't ask in front of everyone. That evening she knocked, sat on my bed, and said, "You don't have to hide this from us."
Then she asked if she could tell my mother. I said yes. My mother came in that same night and held my hand till I fell asleep. The next week, we went to see the school counsellor together.
- Shankar

qa.q: When did Shankar cry after Dadaji died?
qa.a: Every night, under the blanket.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling while crying silently and withdrawing?
qa.a: Shankar felt deep grief and sadness, hiding it from everyone and pulling away from friends.

qa.q: What did Parul do that was right?
qa.a: Parul noticed the signs, spoke privately, told Shankar hiding wasn't needed, and brought in the mother that same night.

qa.q: How might Shankar's friends have seen the missed cricket and texts?
qa.a: They may have thought Shankar was ignoring them, not knowing it was hidden grief.

grounding: The narrator recalls silent crying and withdrawal after a grandfather's death, and a cousin bringing in a trusted adult the same night.

passage:
Warden's note, hostel Block B, Thursday night
At 10.30 pm, Bhavna came to my room. Her roommate, Aditi, has been crying silently under her blanket most nights this week and has stopped going to dinner and to the dance club she loved. I went up with Bhavna straight away. Aditi was curled under the blanket, very still. I sat on the edge of the bed and waited. After a while she said, "Nothing's going to get better here." I did not argue or lecture. I said I was glad Bhavna had come for me, that Aditi was not in any trouble, and that I would stay. With her agreement I phoned her mother that night, and they talked for twenty minutes. I checked on her again at midnight; she was asleep. Next steps: the counsellor will see her at 8 am, and I have told Bhavna to come to me any time.

qa.q: What time did Bhavna come to the warden's room?
qa.a: At 10.30 pm.

qa.q: What might Aditi's words "Nothing's going to get better here" suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Aditi seemed hopeless and lonely, worn down after a week of hidden crying and pulling back from dinner and dance.

qa.q: Which of the warden's steps mattered most that night?
qa.a: Going up at once, staying calmly without lecturing, phoning Aditi's mother that night, checking again at midnight, and booking the counsellor for the morning.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt going to the warden?
qa.a: Bhavna was probably worried about Aditi and unsure whether speaking up was right; the warden's quick response showed it was.

grounding: It shows a teenager's frequent silent crying with withdrawal and hopeless words being taken to a trusted adult who responds the same night and involves a counsellor.
